question: Teacher has a BS in elementary ed from an NC-approved program, passed Praxis, and is in year 2 of a Residency License. Can they move to a CPL now or do they need more time?

answer.summary: The teacher can convert to a CPL only after meeting every CPL requirement, and the most important one is three years of licensed teaching experience, which a teacher in year 2 of a residency license may not yet have. The passages do not say whether residency-license years count toward that experience, so confirm the teacher's actual years and test scores before deciding; the conversion, if completed by June 30 of year 3, takes effect July 1 of the following fiscal year.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued under LICN-019.
To convert a residency license to a CPL, the applicant must meet the CPL requirements in LICN-024 and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

A teacher CPL requires holding an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, satisfying the licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completing a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

The Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement does not apply if the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina, or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL.

The teacher has held the residency license for two years, so the three-year CPL experience requirement is not met by the residency period alone unless the passages' definition of licensed teaching experience counts residency years. The passages do not define 'licensed teaching experience' or say whether residency years count, so this cannot be confirmed from the policies provided.

Conversion timing: if the applicant satisfies the requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the CPL is effective on the date requirements are met.

For elementary (K-6) licensure, the required tests are Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a required score of 233, and either Pearson Test 203 Mathematics or Praxis Test 7813 CKT Math with a required score of 227 or 150 respectively.

To renew a residency license for the next year, the employing PSU must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized EPP, is employed as a teacher in the PSU, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed the 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license.

questions_for_user: How many years of licensed teaching experience does the teacher have in total, including any years in other jurisdictions, and how many of those count as licensed teaching?
Which required tests were passed (Pearson 890 Foundations of Reading and the math test), and what were the scores? The table requires Pearson 890 for reading, not Praxis.
Did the teacher complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program, or does an exception apply (three years of licensed teaching experience outside NC, or a prior reverted CPL)?
Is the teacher currently enrolled in a recognized EPP, and has the EPP recommended the teacher for the CPL?
Has the teacher completed the required 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license?
Is the teacher currently employed by the PSU in the residency license area?
not_covered: Whether time spent on a residency license counts toward the three years of licensed teaching experience required for a CPL.
The definition of 'licensed teaching experience' and how partial years are counted.
Whether the BS from an NC-approved program alone satisfies the EPP recommendation requirement for conversion.
The exact details of the Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016, which is referenced but not provided.
Whether the teacher's test results from the Praxis (rather than Pearson) satisfy the reading requirement, since the table lists Pearson 890 for reading.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the same needs_more_info verdict as the key, covers the three-year experience requirement, the EPP recommendation, BTSP exceptions, exam requirements, and timing, and asks for the right facts. Claim 4 leans on the teacher's two years, which the cited text does not address, so it is only partially supported.

question: Teacher holds a CPL in middle grades ELA and wants to add a Spanish K-12 area. They have 18 graduate credits in Spanish. Do the credits qualify?

answer.summary: The 18 graduate credits do not meet the coursework route for adding Spanish K-12, which requires 24 credit hours from an institution of higher education with a grade of C or better in each course. The teacher would need 6 more qualifying credit hours or must satisfy the Spanish licensure examination requirement instead.

claims.text: Spanish K-12 is a special subject area license under LICN-010, so it can be added to an existing license.

A teacher with a CPL may request to add a new license area to an existing CPL. Coursework alone can add an area only if the applicant completes 24 credit hours from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course.

The alternative route is to satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for the license area. For Spanish K-12 (code 521), that is Praxis 5195 with a required score of 168, or ACTFL OPI & WPT at Advanced Low.
Arithmetic: the coursework route requires 24 credit hours. The teacher has 18, so they are 6 credit hours short (24 − 18 = 6). The 18 credits alone do not satisfy LICN-013 §1(b).

LICN-013 §2 bars the coursework-only route for Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum. Spanish is not on that list, so coursework is an available route for Spanish if the 24-hour requirement is met.
The 18-credit threshold in LICN-006 applies to graduate salary pay, not to adding a license area. It does not satisfy LICN-013.

questions_for_user: Were all 18 graduate credits earned at an institution of higher education, and were they all in Spanish coursework?
Did the teacher earn a grade of C or better in each of the 18 credits?
Does the teacher have, or can they complete, 6 more qualifying Spanish credit hours (for 24 total)?
Has the teacher taken the Praxis 5195 or the ACTFL OPI and WPT, and if so, what were the scores?
Does the teacher hold an IPL or CPL in good standing for the add-on request? LICN-013 covers both.
premise_corrections: The question implies the 18 graduate credits might qualify for the Spanish add-on. Under LICN-013 §1(b), the coursework route requires 24 credit hours, not 18.
not_covered: The passages do not state whether graduate-level credits are treated differently from undergraduate credits for the 24-hour add-on requirement.
The passages do not explain how a 24-credit-hour count is verified or how transcripts are submitted.
The passages do not describe any fee, processing time, or application form for adding a license area.
The passages do not describe whether credits earned before a particular date are accepted.
The passages do not describe any exception that would reduce the 24-credit-hour requirement.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the correct verdict: 18 graduate credits fall short of the 24-hour coursework requirement, and it gives the Praxis 5195 and ACTFL alternatives. Its claims are well backed by the cited LICN-013, LICN-003, and LICN-006 text, though the LICN-010 citation only shows Spanish in a list and it omits the $60 fee and the explicit point that graduate credits are not restricted.

question: Teacher is on a Permit to Teach in Spanish, has 90 credits, no degree yet. Can they add an elementary license later?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: Not on the current Permit to Teach: DPI cannot add a license area to a permit, and elementary can only be added by passing the licensure examination, not by coursework. A later add-on is possible only if the teacher first holds an IPL or CPL and then passes the elementary exam. The permit itself also appears inconsistent with the facts, since a permit requires a bachelor's degree.

claims.text: A permit to teach may be requested only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license.
A permit to teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.
DPI shall not add additional teaching license areas under the add-on rule to a Permit to Teach.
Add-on areas may be requested only for an existing initial professional license (IPL) or continuing professional license (CPL).
Elementary Education can be added only by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements; it cannot be added through coursework alone.

For other areas, an add-on may be made by passing the licensure exam or by completing 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course. This coursework route does not apply to Elementary Education.

The teacher's 90 credits do not count toward the Elementary add-on, because the policies allow Elementary only through the examination and the coursework route excludes it. The policies provided do not state how general credit hours count toward a degree or license.
The Spanish permit is a teaching license area (Secondary Spanish), so the permit is tied to that area.

An IPL may be issued to an applicant who completed a recognized NC educator preparation program and was recommended by the EPP, or who completed an out-of-state EPP, or who holds an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience there.

questions_for_user: Does the teacher hold a bachelor's degree? The permit rule requires one, and the teacher is described as having no degree yet.
Has the teacher ever been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license? A permit is available only if not.
Does the teacher currently hold an IPL or CPL, or is one expected? An elementary add-on requires one.
Has the teacher completed a recognized educator preparation program, and in what level (Bachelor's, Master's, etc.)?
Has the teacher passed the Elementary Education licensure examination, or are they planning to take it?
premise_corrections: The question assumes the teacher can hold a Permit to Teach with no degree. The passages say a permit requires at least a bachelor's degree, so the current permit may not be valid as described.
not_covered: Whether 90 credits count toward a bachelor's degree or any other licensure requirement.
The specific Elementary Education licensure exam and passing score.
Whether the teacher's Spanish permit was properly issued or what happens if the teacher lacks a degree.
Any rule on what happens when a permit expires on June 30 and the teacher has no other license.
Whether the teacher may keep teaching Spanish after the permit expires.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line that the Spanish permit cannot be used to add Elementary, and that Elementary requires an IPL or CPL plus the exam rather than coursework. It hedges with a 'conditional' verdict where the key is definite, and it omits the emergency and residency license points.

question: candidate with out of state license, 4 yrs exp, middle grades math. what NC license and what's missing
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: If the candidate's 4 years are licensed professional educator experience, the policies point to a Continuing Professional License (CPL) under LICN-025 §2, not an Initial Professional License. The CPL requires a clear out-of-state license plus either NBPTS certification or substantially similar licensure requirements, which includes passing the out-of-state exam for middle grades math. Several facts needed to decide this are not in the analyst's description.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license (CPL). A candidate with 4 years exceeds the three-year threshold, so the CPL section applies, provided the 4 years are licensed professional educator experience.
The initial professional license (IPL) pathway is for an out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience, so it does not fit a 4-year candidate.

To qualify for a CPL, the applicant must meet both criteria: (a) hold a clear license from another jurisdiction, and (b) either hold NBPTS certification or have licensure requirements in the other jurisdiction that are substantially similar to North Carolina's.

A clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined by that jurisdiction, free of any pending unprofessional conduct investigation in any state, and not voluntarily surrendered while under investigation.

Substantially similar means the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of an EPP recognized by the state where the EPP is located, and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought under LICN-010.

Middle grades math is a North Carolina license area under LICN-010 (Middle Grades, Mathematics). The exam requirement for that area is Praxis test 5164 with a required score of 157, unless the candidate meets the CPL route through an out-of-state exam.

For a CPL based on an out-of-state exam, the applicant must present the exam results at the time of initial North Carolina licensure. Out-of-state exam results cannot be used to convert an IPL to a CPL.

An out-of-state applicant is one who completed an educator preparation program whose principal place of business is outside North Carolina. The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where the EPP is based.
The number of years of professional experience is printed on the NC license, so the years confirmed for this candidate will be recorded there.

If the candidate is an active-duty servicemember or a spouse of one, out-of-state exam scores need not come from the same jurisdiction where the EPP was completed. The passages do not say whether this candidate qualifies for that provision.

questions_for_user: Are all 4 years licensed professional educator experience in the out-of-state license, or is some of it unlicensed or in another position?
Is the out-of-state license clear: in good standing, renewable, never revoked or disciplined, with no pending unprofessional conduct investigation, and not surrendered under investigation?
Does the candidate hold NBPTS certification? If not, were the other state's requirements substantially similar to NC's (EPP completion and a passing out-of-state exam)?

Did the candidate pass the other state's exam for middle grades math, and what was the score and which jurisdiction issued it? Does it match NC's Praxis 5164 score of 157 for the area, or is the exam from a jurisdiction the policies do not address?
Which state is the EPP located in, and is that EPP recognized by its state's licensing authority?
Is the candidate an active-duty servicemember or a spouse of one?
premise_corrections: Only licensed professional educator experience counts toward the three-year threshold in LICN-025 §2. The passages do not say whether unlicensed or non-educator years count.
not_covered: The CPL application fee. LICN-008 lists fees for an out-of-state initial professional license ($100) but no CPL fee.
Whether a specific out-of-state exam passed by this candidate is recognized as equivalent to NC's middle grades math exam, beyond the LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) requirement.
How the SBE determines that another jurisdiction's requirements are substantially similar.
Details of NBPTS certification requirements and whether the candidate's NBPTS status is valid.
Whether the candidate's middle grades math license would also need a separate test or area addition under LICN-013.

incorrect_statements: Claim 8 says the candidate's years of professional experience are printed on the NC license, but the cited LICN-001 §3(c)(ii) only lists years of professional experience as an applicant item and says nothing about the license printing them.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line: 4 years exceeds the IPL limit, so the CPL under LICN-025 §2 applies, with the clear-license, substantially-similar, and exam requirements correctly stated. It omits the LICN-010 degree-level rule and the LICN-020 §1(b) alternative IPL route for an out-of-state EPP, and it includes one unsupported claim about the license printing years of experience.

question: Applicant completed a teacher prep program in the Philippines, has a teaching license there, wants to teach math in NC. Which NC license could they start with?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The applicant could likely start on an Initial Professional License under LICN-020 §1(b) or §1(c), depending on their years of licensed teaching experience, but the choice and the math license area depend on facts not yet given: grade band, degree level, years of experience, and whether the Philippine program is recognized. Permit to Teach is a possible stopgap only if they hold a bachelor's degree and have never held an NC license.

claims.text: A program completed outside North Carolina makes the applicant an out-of-state applicant, including international preparation programs.
An applicant may qualify for an Initial Professional License by having completed an EPP based outside North Carolina.

An applicant may also qualify for an Initial Professional License by holding a clear license from a jurisdiction outside North Carolina and having fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction. Whether the applicant's Philippine license is a clear license is not addressed in the passages.

Any EPP required for a license must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. Whether the applicant's Philippine program meets this is not addressed in the passages.

A teacher license is available only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP (Bachelor's, Master's, Specialist, or Doctoral). The applicant's degree level therefore determines the highest license level they can receive.

Math (Kindergarten through Grade 6) is an add-on classification that cannot be issued as a standalone license and can only be added to an existing license. The math license area therefore depends on the grade band and the applicant's existing license.
An Initial Professional License entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

If the applicant has more than three years of licensed professional educator experience and holds a clear out-of-state license, they may qualify for a Continuing Professional License directly. This requires either NBPTS certification or out-of-state requirements substantially similar to NC's, meaning completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on the applicable exam for each license area sought.

A permit to teach may be requested by a school unit only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license. It is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

Test requirements for NC licenses are set by the SBE, and the math testing requirements are listed by license area and code. The applicable test and score for the applicant's grade band are needed; the passage table is incomplete for the math areas.

questions_for_user: What grade band is the applicant targeting for math (Kindergarten through Grade 6, Grades 6 through 12, or another band)?
What is the highest degree the applicant completed through the Philippine teacher preparation program (bachelor's, master's, specialist, or doctoral)?
How many years of licensed teaching experience does the applicant have in the Philippines, and is their Philippine license a clear license in good standing?
Is the Philippine teacher preparation program recognized by the Philippine licensing authority, and has it been reviewed for SBE recognition?
Does the applicant already hold any North Carolina professional educator license?
Has the applicant taken or passed any licensure exam, and if so, which test and score?
not_covered: Whether the Philippine teacher preparation program is recognized by the SBE or by the Philippine licensing authority under LICN-001 §3(d).
Whether a foreign clear license qualifies as a clear license under LICN-025 §2(a) for the applicant's specific license.

Whether the applicant must pass NC licensure exams before receiving an Initial Professional License under LICN-020 §1(b) or §1(c). LICN-020 §2 addresses exam deferral only for NC-recognized EPP completers.
The specific NC math test requirement and score for the applicant's grade band. The LICN-003 §5 table is incomplete in the passages provided.
Credential evaluation or equivalency rules for foreign degrees and foreign licenses.
Math license areas for Grades 6 through 12 and the requirements for those areas.
Whether the applicant qualifies for a Residency License, and its requirements beyond the professional development section.
Any policy on how Philippine teaching experience is credited for salary purposes.

incorrect_statements: The LICN-003 §5 math test passage table is said to be incomplete for math areas, but the cited table lists Mathematics K-6 Pearson 203/CKT options, Mathematics middle grades code 78200 with Praxis 5164 at 157, and Mathematics secondary code 200 with Praxis 5165 at 159.

The answer omits that an IPL applicant must pass the math exam (out-of-state exam or NC test before or during the third year after a first-year attempt), and instead says it is unclear whether exams are required before an IPL.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's needs_more_info verdict and correctly identifies the IPL routes under LICN-020 §1(b)/(c), the EPP recognition requirement, and the degree-level limit. It misses the IPL math exam requirement and the specific NC math test scores, wrongly says the math test table is incomplete, and omits the emergency, residency, and J-1 international faculty alternatives.

question: A teacher holds a current South Carolina professional license in high school biology with 6 years of experience and a master's in biology. Which NC license applies, and does the master's change anything?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The passages support a Secondary Biology teacher license (LICN-010) but do not name the NC license type an out-of-state applicant would receive, so the exact license cannot be confirmed from them. The master's changes the outcome only if it was completed through an educator preparation program (EPP) at the master's level; otherwise it may affect graduate salary pay only if LICN-006 criteria are met.

claims.text: Biology is a secondary (Grades 9-12) teacher license area in North Carolina.
A teacher license entitles the licensee to teach in the license area(s) indicated on the license.
To qualify for a teacher license, an applicant must have completed an EPP at the Bachelor's (A), Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level.

An applicant is eligible only for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. A master's degree therefore leads to an M-level license only if it was completed through an EPP; a master's that was not an EPP does not raise the license level, though the applicant may still qualify for graduate salary pay under LICN-006.

Any license requiring EPP completion must be from an EPP recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. Whether the applicant's EPP meets this is not established by the analyst's facts.
A person who completed an EPP with a principal place of business outside North Carolina is an out-of-state applicant.

Graduate salary pay on the master's level requires: (a) the master's from an accredited institution (or accredited when conferred); (b) the degree directly related to an existing area of licensure or current assignment; and (c) at least 50% of the school day assigned in the area for which the degree applies.
The SBE's approved test for Secondary Biology (license code 310) is Praxis 5236 with a required score of 154.
Out-of-state applicants must submit proof of any current, valid educator license from another state.
The fee for an Out-of-State Initial Professional License application is $100 for applications opened effective January 1, 2017.

Experience credit is calculated at one year per fiscal year of full-time work of at least six calendar months in a school unit; part-time work requires at least 15 hours per week, and partial years may be combined. Six years of experience counts as six years only if each year meets these rules.

An out-of-state teacher with at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina may be exempt from the Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement for a continuing professional license, but this applies to CPL qualification rather than initial licensing.

questions_for_user: Was the master's in biology completed through an educator preparation program (EPP), or was it a content degree outside an EPP? This determines whether it can raise the license level to M-level under LICN-010 §3.
Is the master's from an accredited institution, and is its subject directly related to biology? Will the teacher spend at least 50% of the school day teaching biology?
Has the teacher passed the Praxis 5236 (score 154) or another applicable licensure examination for biology?
Were the six years of South Carolina experience full-time school-unit service of at least six calendar months per fiscal year, or part-time at 15+ hours per week?
Is the South Carolina license currently valid, and does it have any suspension, revocation, or criminal history disclosures under LICN-004 §1(h)?
Is the teacher seeking an initial NC license, and has the teacher previously held any NC professional educator license (relevant to LICN-017 permit eligibility)?
premise_corrections: The question asks which NC license applies, but the passages do not list an out-of-state reciprocity pathway or specify which NC license type (e.g., initial professional license or residency license) an SC-licensed teacher receives, so the premise that a specific NC license is determined cannot be fully confirmed from these policies.
not_covered: The NC license type (initial professional license, residency, or other) issued to an out-of-state teacher with an existing out-of-state license.
Whether the South Carolina license is recognized for NC licensure or what reciprocity or transcript evaluation applies.
Whether South Carolina teaching experience counts toward NC experience credit for salary, and how out-of-state experience is documented.
Whether the master's degree was issued by an EPP recognized under LICN-001 §3(d); the passages do not establish EPP status for the master's program.
Requirements for SC-licensed teachers beyond the passages provided (e.g., TCED-016 Beginning Teacher Support Program details).

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer's needs_more_info verdict and its master's-degree analysis (EPP-dependent license level, salary pay under LICN-006) match the key. It omits the likely Continuing Professional License classification, the LICN-025 clear-license and NBPTS/substantially-similar requirements, and the six-year threshold reasoning, and it leaves the license type unresolved. Most cited claims are backed by their policy text, though claim 11 cites nothing about CPL or BTSP exemption.

question: Teacher with an expired CPL, lapsed 14 months ago, wants to return to classroom. What's the reinstatement path?

answer.summary: The passages do not provide a reinstatement path for an expired CPL. The only route they describe for an expired CPL is a PSU-requested validation under LICN-033 §3, which depends on whether the teacher was employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year and on whether a PSU will sponsor the request. The reinstatement process in LICN-007 §8 applies to revoked licenses or denied applications, not expired ones.

claims.text: The passages do not describe a reinstatement process for an expired continuing professional license.

LICN-007 §8 allows an individual whose license was revoked, or whose application was denied, to petition for reinstatement or reconsideration no sooner than 12 months after the effective date of the revocation or denial, by written petition to the Superintendent. If the teacher's license only expired, this section does not appear to apply, and it would matter only if the license was revoked or the application was denied.

A license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire, unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy. The exact expiration date is needed to place the 14-month lapse in a fiscal year.

A PSU governing body may ask DPI to validate an expired CPL issued under its employment, even if the educator lacks the required CEUs, but only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.

A validated CPL is effective for three years. To renew it for a new five-year cycle, the educator must complete the renewal requirements in LICN-030, LICN-031, or LICN-032 by the end of the third year.

Under LICN-030 §2(b)(iv), a teacher who meets the Section 1 renewal criteria but is not placed on a mandatory improvement plan by the employing LSAU has the license expire at the end of the renewal cycle. That teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving DPI's notice of expiration. This route is tied to the employing LSAU's decision in the final year of a cycle, so it may not apply to a teacher who lapsed 14 months ago.

A mandatory improvement plan that results in an IPL requires a current CPL, a teacher in the final year of a renewal cycle, and an employing LSAU that places the teacher on the plan. A license that lapsed 14 months ago would likely not meet these conditions.
An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license. A CPL is a five-year, renewable license.

questions_for_user: Was the CPL allowed to expire through non-renewal, or was it revoked or the application denied? Revocation or denial would bring in LICN-007 §8 instead.
What is the exact expiration date of the CPL? This determines the fiscal years involved.
Was the teacher employed by any North Carolina PSU during the fiscal year before the validation request? LICN-033 §3 turns on this.
Was the CPL originally issued under employment by a specific PSU, and will that PSU's governing body sponsor a validation request now?
Does the teacher currently have an offer of employment with a PSU, and in what license area and grade band?
Did the teacher complete the required CEUs during the last cycle, and what was their most recent annual evaluation rating?
Has the teacher received a DPI notice of expiration, and on what date?
premise_corrections: The question refers to a reinstatement path. The passages provide reinstatement only for revoked licenses or denied applications under LICN-007 §8. For an expired CPL, the passages describe validation under LICN-033 §3 instead.
not_covered: Any reinstatement or reactivation procedure specific to an expired CPL beyond LICN-033 §3 and LICN-030 §2(b)(iv).
Whether an educator who lapsed and is not validated can obtain a new IPL or CPL, and what requirements apply (beyond the general language in LICN-030 §2(b)(iv)).
CEU requirements that would apply to a validated CPL before renewal, beyond the cross-references to LICN-030, LICN-031, and LICN-032 (LICN-031 and LICN-032 were not provided).
Whether the Beginning Teacher Support Program or licensure examination requirements apply to a returning educator.
Exact fiscal-year mapping for the 14-month lapse, since the expiration date was not provided.
Any rules in effect before 2026-07-01 that may have applied when the license expired. The provided versions are current only.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gets the bottom line right: LICN-007 §8 covers only revoked or denied licenses, and validation under LICN-033 §3 depends on whether the teacher was employed by a PSU in the preceding fiscal year. It omits the $60 fee, the specific CEU and proficiency renewal requirements, and the April 15 timing point, but every claim is backed by its cited text.

question: Candidate has a master's in school counseling from an out of state program, 2 yrs counseling experience in another state. What NC school counselor license do they qualify for?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: Based on 2 years of out-of-state experience and an out-of-state master's, the candidate would fall under the Student Services Personnel license (School Counselor classification) at the M-level, most likely as an initial professional license (IPL), not a continuing professional license. Whether they qualify depends on whether they held a clear out-of-state license in school counseling, whether the 2 years was licensed professional educator experience, whether their EPP is recognized, and their School Counselor exam status.

claims.text: NC has no separate 'school counselor license' in these policies. School counselor is one classification (School Counselor, §2(a)) of the Student Services Personnel license, which is 5-year renewable and is issued under LICN-012.

To qualify for a student services personnel license, the applicant must have completed an EPP at the master's (M), specialist (S), or doctoral (D) level. A master's in school counseling meets the M-level requirement, and the license is issued at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.
The license will show the applicant's degree level, based on the highest degree issued by an EPP, and years of professional experience.

An EPP for a license that requires program completion must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. Whether the out-of-state program is recognized must be confirmed.

Out-of-state applicants with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an IPL if they either hold a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or completed an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where the EPP is based. At 2 years, the candidate is under the 3-year threshold.
Alternatively, an initial professional license may be requested for a North Carolina-trained applicant, but this path is not relevant here because the candidate completed an out-of-state program.

A CPL for out-of-state applicants requires more than three years of licensed professional educator experience, so 2 years does not qualify for a CPL under LICN-025 §2. The candidate would be on the IPL track unless the experience situation changes.

School Counselor is listed in the NC testing requirements under license code 005 with required test Praxis 5422 and a required score of 159. The candidate must meet this requirement, or its out-of-state equivalent, to satisfy licensure examination requirements.

For an out-of-state IPL in a license area other than Elementary Education or Special Education: General Curriculum, the applicant must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the NC exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having attempted them at least once during the first year.
Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial licensure in NC. Out-of-state exam results cannot be used to convert an IPL to a CPL.

The out-of-state exam scores for an active-duty servicemember or spouse need not come from the jurisdiction where the EPP was completed. This applies only if the candidate is a military servicemember or spouse, which is not stated.

Experience counts for a student services personnel license only if it is licensed professional educator experience. Experience credit for salary purposes for non-teaching work is governed separately under LICN-006 §II, which requires a recommendation from the employing LEA's personnel administrator, relevance to the license area, at least 20 hours per week, and completion after age 18.

Documentation required for the application includes official transcripts, EPP completion verification, and documentation of exam performance. If seeking experience credit for prior work, documentation under LICN-006 is also required.

Confirm the grade band, the social studies credit hours or test score, and the 2-year emergency license history, because current rules say an emergency license is valid only through one fiscal year and cannot be renewed.

The passages do not state what G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) requires, so that statutory condition cannot be verified from the policies provided.

If the teacher's grade band is middle grades (6-9), social studies requires Praxis test 5589 with a required score of 149 instead.

An emergency license is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed. Each emergency license therefore covers one fiscal year, and the policy defines an emergency license as a one-year nonrenewable license.

The policies provided are current versions only. A two-year emergency license under current rules would require a separate request for each fiscal year, and the passages cannot confirm what rules applied to any earlier emergency license.

A residency license is a classification of teacher license. The general rule requiring completion of an educator preparation program is subject to an exception in Section 5, which lists residency licenses, so the policies do not require educator preparation for this license.
Whether the teacher's history bachelor's coursework counts toward the 24 hours in the social studies content area is not addressed in the passages.

A public school unit employing a residency license teacher must provide at least 3 hours of field experience before classroom teaching and at least 10 hours over the first year. Field experience may be completed while the teacher holds a permit or emergency license before the first residency year. The unit must also provide 10 days of professional development.

question: Applicant has a BS in special education from a different state, teaching EC in another state for 3 years, wants a NC EC license. Which one?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The applicant's path depends on whether they hold a clear out-of-state license, whether they have fewer than, exactly, or more than three years of licensed experience, and which EC license area they want. The policies do not say how to treat exactly three years, so the analyst should confirm the exact years and the area before choosing between an IPL and a CPL.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license (IPL) if they either hold a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction or completed an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP is based.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license (CPL) if they hold a clear license from another jurisdiction and either hold NBPTS certification or the other jurisdiction's requirements were substantially similar to North Carolina's.

A clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, not under pending unprofessional conduct investigation, and not voluntarily surrendered while under investigation.
Substantially similar means the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.

Three years is the boundary in both directions: the IPL rule covers fewer than three years and the CPL rule covers more than three years. The policies do not state which rule applies at exactly three years of licensed experience.

For an IPL in Special Education: General Curriculum, the applicant must satisfy the applicable NC licensure exam requirements by the end of the third year of licensure, regardless of any out-of-state exam passed. For an IPL in any other area, the applicant must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area or satisfy NC exam requirements before or during the third year, provided they attempted the exams at least once in the first year.
Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

NC exam requirements vary by area. For Special Education: General Curriculum (88091), the listed requirements include Test 5355 (score 145), Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading (233), and Pearson Test 203 Mathematics or CKT 7813 (227 or 150). Other EC areas have different tests.
A teacher license is issued at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP, so a bachelor's degree from an EPP corresponds to the A-Level.
An out-of-state applicant who qualifies for a teacher license may add an area based on an out-of-state exam pass, provided results are submitted at initial application.

NC licenses are issued in classifications (Teacher, Administrator, Student Services Personnel), and a license lists the grade levels, content areas, and specializations for which the holder is eligible.
The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where the EPP has its principal place of business.

questions_for_user: Does the applicant currently hold a clear professional educator license in the other state that is in good standing, renewable, and free of discipline or pending investigations?
Is the applicant's licensed teaching experience fewer than three years, exactly three years, or more than three years? Exactly three years is not addressed by the policies.

Which specific NC EC license area is sought (for example, Special Education: General Curriculum 88091, Adapted Curriculum 88092, Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled 88085, Cross Categorical 88001, or another)?
Did the applicant pass the other state's exam for that EC area, and what was the score?
Was the BS program an EPP recognized by the other state's licensing authority?
Does the applicant hold NBPTS certification?
Does the applicant hold any degree beyond the BS, such as a master's?
Did the applicant's other state require a recognized EPP and an exam for the license area (the substantially similar test)?
not_covered: How the policies treat exactly three years of licensed experience, since the IPL rule covers fewer than three years and the CPL rule covers more than three years.
Whether experience in the other state counts as licensed professional educator experience under LICN-025 when the applicant had a license only in a different category.
Which out-of-state exam scores satisfy NC requirements for each EC area, beyond the NC test table.
The NC EC license areas' requirements in full detail beyond the listed tests, including any requirements for the Adapted Curriculum or other special areas.
Any rules on the time limit for converting an IPL to a regular license beyond the three-year exam deadline.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly returns needs_more_info, flags that exactly three years is not addressed, and its claims are all backed by the cited policy text. It does not state that three years falls outside both the LICN-025 §1 and §2 thresholds, misses the LICN-020 §1(b) versus LICN-025 conflict, and omits the LICN-024 CPL path and the other classification options.

question: Teacher is an administrator candidate with an MSA, 3 years as assistant principal in SC, wants NC principal license. Eligible?

answer.summary: The passages do not give a yes or no on eligibility yet. claims.text: To qualify for an administrator license other than Exceptional Children or superintendent, an applicant must have completed an administrator preparation program at the Master's, Specialist, or Doctoral level.
For a principal license, the master's degree must be in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or another education-related field.
An administrator preparation program (APP) is a program approved by the State Board of Education to prepare, train, and recommend administrator candidates.
An applicant is eligible only for an administrator license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP or APP.
Principal is an administrator license classification.
The passages list the principal licensure test as the North Carolina Principal Portfolio Assessment, with a required score of 'Completion with validated score' and a test code marked TBD.

An applicant for an administrator license must satisfy any applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, provided the applicant attempts the examination at least once during the first year of licensure.
If the applicant does not satisfy the examination requirements before initial application but otherwise meets the qualifications, DPI issues an initial professional license.
An out-of-state applicant is one who completed an EPP or APP with a principal place of business outside North Carolina, including international programs.

The out-of-state IPL path in LICN-025 §1(a) applies to an out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience. The candidate's three years as an assistant principal in SC is at the threshold, so this path may not apply, and the passages do not address out-of-state applicants with three or more years.
Assistant principals in a public school unit must hold either a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license.
An EPP that requires completion must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business.

A CPL based on a clear license in another jurisdiction requires meeting LICN-025. For administrators, CPL also requires satisfying applicable exam requirements and meeting other LICN-011 requirements.

claims.text: NC professional educator licenses are issued in classifications that include Teacher, Administrator, and Student Services Personnel, and any person employed as a professional educator in a NC public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license.
Birth – Kindergarten is one of the teacher license classifications under LICN-010.

The Pre-School Add-On is a separate classification. It cannot be issued as a standalone license and may only be added to an existing Elementary, Special Education, or Family and Consumer Sciences – General license.
The NC testing table lists Birth through Kindergarten (license code 14) with no required tests and no required score.

A teacher license entitles the licensee to teach in the license area(s) shown on the license, and a teacher license requires completion of an EPP at the Bachelor's, Master's, Specialist, or Doctoral level.
An applicant is eligible only for a license at the highest degree level at which they completed an EPP.

For any license requiring EPP completion, the EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. Virginia is outside NC, so the applicant is an out-of-state applicant.
An NC license application must include proof of any current and valid educator license from another state, and documentation of any applicable licensure examination performance.
An Initial Professional License (IPL) entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in NC.

A Continuing Professional License (CPL) requires holding an IPL or residency license in NC, plus at least three years of licensed teaching experience, plus completing the examination requirements and a Beginning Teacher Support Program, unless exempt. Exemption applies to three or more years of licensed teaching outside NC.

A permit to teach may be requested by a PSU for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license. A permit is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

If the teacher is an active-duty servicemember or a spouse, NC employment in a licensed position requires either applying for an NC license or obtaining recognition of a covered license under federal law.

question: Career changer, 10 yrs as a nurse, has BS in nursing, wants to teach CTE health science. What license do they start with?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The passages do not name one starting license for this career changer. The answer turns on whether they completed an educator preparation program (EPP) and at what degree level, and whether they have ever held an NC professional educator license. If they have not, a Permit to Teach is available only through a request from the hiring school unit, and it does not raise pay based on their nursing experience.

claims.text: A teacher license requires completion of an educator preparation program at one of the listed degree levels, Bachelor's (A) through Doctoral (D), except as provided in Section 5, which is not included in the passages.
An applicant is eligible only for a license at the highest degree level at which they completed an EPP. Graduate salary pay may still be available under LICN-006.
Career and Technical Education is a license classification, and the CTE list includes Health Sciences Education – Registered Nurse and Health Sciences Education – Non-Registered Nurse.
An applicant with only a high school diploma or associate's degree may be issued a CTE license, but this applicant holds a bachelor's degree, so that provision does not determine their level.

A Permit to Teach may be requested by the governing body of a public school unit for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license.
A Permit to Teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year it was requested for and cannot be extended or renewed.

For State Salary Schedule pay, a Permit to Teach is set at the bachelor's (A-Level) zero-years level regardless of education or prior work experience, so the 10 years of nursing would not count toward pay under a permit.
Permits, emergency, residency, limited, provisional, and certain other license classifications cannot have additional teaching areas added under LICN-013.

An Initial Professional License (IPL) is a three-year nonrenewable license. A CPL requires holding an IPL or residency license in NC, plus three years of licensed teaching experience and a Beginning Teacher Support Program (unless exempt).

Non-teaching work experience may be credited toward the licensure experience rating for salary purposes if it is directly related to the area of licensure, was at least half-time (20 or more hours per week), and was completed after age 18, on the recommendation of the hiring LEA's designated personnel administrator. question: CTE teacher with an industry credential in welding and 5000 hours on the job. Which CTE license level can they get?

answer.summary: The passages let a CTE welding teacher hold a teaching license without a bachelor's degree, since CTE is one of the areas open to high school or associate's-level applicants. The license level itself is set by the applicant's degree and EPP completion, not by work hours or an industry credential. The 5000 hours can only count toward salary experience credit if they meet the non-teaching work criteria, and the passages give no hours-to-years conversion, so the analyst needs to confirm the degree, the program, and the nature of the hours.

claims.text: A teacher license for Career and Technical Education can be issued to an applicant with a high school diploma (or equivalent) or an associate's degree (V-Level), provided the applicant meets all other requirements for the license classification sought.
Welding is listed as a Trade and Industrial Education license area under Career and Technical Education.

Except for the CTE and other exceptions in Section 4, an applicant must complete an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A), Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level to qualify for a teacher license, and is only eligible at the highest degree level completed at an EPP.

The license level is therefore determined by the applicant's highest degree completed through an EPP. Industry credentials and work hours are not listed among the qualifications that set the teacher license level in the passages.

Non-teaching work experience can be credited toward total licensure experience for salary purposes only on the recommendation of the employing personnel administrator. The experience must be at least half-time (20 hours or more per week), completed after age 18, not on-the-job training, paid and documented, and directly related to the license area.

Credit for non-teaching work experience is one year for every two years of full-time relevant experience completed before the bachelor's degree, and one year for every year of full-time relevant experience completed after it. For Class V Career-Technical Trade and Industry licenses, the year count runs from completing the required training and work experience for the provisional license.

Arithmetic on the 5000 hours cannot be completed from the passages. The passages do not define a full-time year in hours, so the 5000 hours cannot be converted to years of credit. Partial-year rules in §I(c) and §II refer to months and equivalence to full-time, not to a set hour count.
Experience years appear on the license as information, but the passages describe experience credit as a salary matter and do not tie it to the license level.

An applicant qualifies only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. For this applicant that is the master's level, so the MSW is the relevant credential.

question: Teacher has a CPL in K-6, wants to add a middle grades science area. Has 12 semester hours in science. Enough?

answer.summary: Twelve semester hours is not enough by itself. Adding Middle Grades Science through coursework requires 24 credit hours with a grade of C or better in each course, so 12 more hours would be needed. The teacher could instead add the area by passing the required exam (Praxis 5442, score 152).

claims.text: Middle Grades (Grade 6 – Grade 9) Science is a teaching license classification under LICN-010 §6(b)(iii).

A CPL holder may request an additional license area if they meet one of two routes: satisfy the licensure examination requirements for that area, or complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the area with a grade of C or better in each course.

Coursework arithmetic: 24 required credit hours minus 12 completed semester hours leaves 12 credit hours still needed, and each of those courses must be a grade of C or better. Only the coursework route is shortfall-based; the exam route does not depend on the 12 hours.
The required test for Middle Grades Science (licensure code 78300) is Praxis 5442 with a required score of 152.
Middle Grades Science is not on the list of areas that can be added only by examination, so coursework is an available route for it under LICN-013 §1(b).

The Add-On policy does not allow addition of license areas to Permit to Teach, Emergency, Residency, Limited, Provisional, International Faculty, or CTE Restricted licenses; the teacher's CPL is not on that list.

question: rl holder, 3rd yr, bs in english, never took praxis content test. what happens at end of rl?

answer.summary: At the end of the third year, the residency license (RL) does not automatically become a professional license. It converts to an initial (IPL) or continuing (CPL) professional license only if the applicant meets the IPL or CPL requirements, including EPP recommendation, by June 30 of the third year. If not, the RL expires and the IPL or CPL takes effect only once the requirements are met. The passages do not clearly say how the missing Praxis content test affects conversion, so the analyst needs to confirm the license area, how the RL was issued, and the EPP status before deciding.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019. A third-year RL is therefore the final year of the RL.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024, and must be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

If the applicant meets the conversion requirements by June 30 of the third year of the RL, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If the applicant does not meet them by that date, the RL expires, and the IPL or CPL is effective on the date the applicant meets the requirements.

An IPL requires either completion of a recognized NC EPP with EPP recommendation, completion of an out-of-state EPP, or an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of experience. An IPL can be requested for an applicant who completed all NC EPP requirements but has not satisfied the licensure exam requirements; in that case EPP recommendation is not required.

The RL was presumably issued under the 24-hour coursework path, since the applicant has not passed the exam. The policy allows an RL on either 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passing the applicable exam. The passages do not state which path was used for this applicant.

To convert an IPL to a clear CPL, the licensure exam must be taken at least once during the first year of the license and passed before or during the third year. The passages do not state whether this clock runs from the RL start date or from the IPL start date.

For English, the NC Board-approved testing requirement is Praxis 5038 with a required score of 5038 - 167 under secondary (grades 9-12) licensure code 100. The middle-grades Language Arts test (5047, score 164) is a different license area. The passages do not explain how the 5038 cut score relates to the scoring format.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for a permit to teach or an emergency license in the same license area.

answer.summary: On the facts given, the passages do not show an initial NC license path. For a Secondary Mathematics license (code 200), the required NC test is Praxis 5165 with a required score of 159. The applicant's actual score is not stated, so it must be checked against 159.

Passing the required exam is also a condition for converting an initial professional license to a clear continuing license. The exam must be taken at least once in the first year and passed before or during the third year.
An applicant with a bachelor's degree is eligible only for a license at the bachelor's (A) level, and only if the degree came from a completed EPP.

The application must include official transcripts for degrees and documentation signed by an EPP official verifying completion of an EPP for the license sought. Without an EPP, that documentation cannot be supplied.

question: Teacher holds a Permit to Teach in computer science, teaching under it for 3 years. Can it be renewed?

answer.summary: A Permit to Teach cannot be renewed or extended under LICN-017 §2. The teacher's 3 years of teaching under the permit do not change the renewal answer, because the policy bars renewal and extension of a permit regardless of the holder's work history.
Computer Science and Information Technology Education is a recognized teacher license area (CTE), so the subject area is not a barrier to a different license type.

question: candidate w/ 15 yrs exp in florida, cert in ESOL, wants nc license. which one?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: With 15 years of out-of-state experience, the IPL route is likely closed, so the realistic option is a Continuing Professional License (CPL) under LICN-025 §2, which requires a clear Florida license and either NBPTS certification or Florida requirements substantially similar to NC's. The ESOL area itself can be added later by passing an out-of-state exam, but the passages do not show whether the Florida ESOL certificate matches NC's ESOL license area, so the file needs the facts listed below before choosing a license.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant qualifies for an Initial Professional License (IPL) under LICN-025 §1(a) only if they have fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience. At 15 years, this candidate does not meet that threshold, unless most of that experience was unlicensed.

The IPL route for an applicant who has never held a license is also limited to fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in the other jurisdiction, so it does not fit a candidate with 15 years.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a Continuing Professional License (CPL), but must meet both criteria in LICN-025 §2(a) (a clear license) and LICN-025 §2(b) (NBPTS certification or substantially similar requirements).

A 'clear license' under LICN-025 §2(a) must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, free of any pending unprofessional-conduct investigation in any state, and not surrendered while under investigation. The candidate's Florida credential must meet all five parts.

'Substantially similar' requires that the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of a recognized educator preparation program and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought. If the candidate holds NBPTS certification, §2(b) is met without this comparison.

For a CPL based on an out-of-state exam, the exam results must be presented at the time of initial licensure in NC, and an out-of-state applicant cannot use an out-of-state exam to convert an IPL to a CPL.

ESOL is an NC license area (code 110), with NC test 5362 at a required score of 155. Passing an out-of-state exam in that area can add it to an NC license without a new NC exam, but only for an applicant who already qualifies under LICN-025 §1 or §2, and evidence must be submitted at initial application.

The passages do not say whether a Florida ESOL certificate counts as the 'corresponding license area' under LICN-025 §1(a)(i) or whether it is equivalent for §2(b). That determination is not addressed in the provided policies.

A permit to teach is possible only if the candidate has a bachelor's degree, has never been issued any NC professional license, and is employed by the requesting school unit. It is valid only until June 30 of the requested fiscal year and cannot be extended or renewed, so it is only a temporary option.

For salary purposes, Florida teaching experience counts as one year per fiscal year of full-time work of at least six calendar months in a school unit. Part-time work requires at least 15 hours per week. Whether the candidate's 15 years qualify depends on the months worked each fiscal year, which the analyst has not provided.

question: Teacher is a former military educator with 8 years experience teaching in DoD schools, no NC license. Which NC license applies?
context_ids: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

answer.summary: The passages do not identify one NC license for this teacher. The answer turns on whether the teacher is active duty or a spouse of active duty, whether they hold a clear out-of-state license, where and at what level they completed an EPP, and whether they have ever held an NC license; the 8 years of DoD teaching alone does not settle it, and the three-year limit in the out-of-state IPL route may exclude it.

claims.text: NC professional educator licenses are classified as Teacher, Administrator, or Student Services Personnel, and the teacher license is the classification relevant here.

An initial professional license (IPL) may be issued through one of three routes: completion of a recognized NC EPP with EPP recommendation; completion of an EPP based outside NC; or holding a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

The out-of-state clear-license route (LICN-020 §1(c)) requires fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in the issuing jurisdiction. With 8 years of teaching, that route is met only if the DoD teaching was not licensed teaching in that jurisdiction, or if the teaching was not in a licensed capacity; the passages do not say whether DoD school service counts as licensed teaching experience in a jurisdiction.

An applicant to a teacher license must have completed an educator preparation program at Bachelor's, Master's, Specialist, or Doctoral level, and is eligible only at the highest degree level completed through an EPP.
An EPP completed for a license must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where the EPP has its principal place of business.

A permit to teach may be requested by a school unit for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license. A permit is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.
A limited license is a three-year renewable license for an individual who has completed an EPP but has not satisfied the applicable licensure examination requirements.

An IPL may be requested by a school unit for an applicant who completed all requirements for a recognized NC EPP but has not met the exam requirements, and in that case the EPP recommendation is not required.

A continuing professional teacher license requires first holding an NC IPL or residency license, meeting exam requirements before or during the third year, at least three years of NC licensed teaching experience, and a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies. It is therefore not an initial option for this teacher.

The active-duty servicemember and spouse provisions apply to a servicemember on full-time active duty, or the spouse of one, whose duty station is in NC. A former servicemember who is no longer on active duty is not covered by these provisions based on the passages. Recognition of an out-of-state covered license also requires relocation to NC on military orders and a covered license that is in good standing with no discipline or pending investigation.

Under the military instructional-role credit for salary purposes, one year of experience credit is awarded for every two years of full-time instructional duties on active military duty, but only for veterans first employed by an NC LEA or charter school on or after July 1, 2014, and only if the service is honorable and verifiable on government service documents. This is a salary rule, not a licensure rule, and does not establish the license itself.
Years of professional experience and degree level are printed on the license, with degree level based on the highest degree issued by an EPP.
